CausalChain: Chronic liver fibrosis -> Increased matrix stiffness -> Activation of integrin β5/FAK/MEK/ERK and YAP/TAZ signaling in TAMs -> Upregulation of HIF‐1α and LOXL2 -> Metabolic reprogramming (fatty acid oxidation and enhanced glycolysis) -> Increased PD‐L1 expression on TAMs -> Suppression of CD8+ T cell cytotoxicity -> Tumor progression
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in the fibrotic liver, the increased extracellular matrix stiffness—acting both alone and in synergy with inflammatory cytokines—triggers a dual mechanotransduction cascade in tumor-associated macrophages. This cascade involves activation of integrin β5‐mediated FAK/MEK/ERK and YAP/TAZ signaling pathways, which in turn upregulate HIF‐1α and LOXL2. These events drive a metabolic reprogramming in TAMs, characterized by increased fatty acid oxidation and glycolysis, leading to enhanced PD‐L1 expression. The consequent suppression of CD8+ T cell cytotoxicity promotes tumor progression. We further propose that the practical implementation of this hypothesis can be achieved using advanced bioengineering tools (such as tunable 3D hydrogels), precise gene-editing techniques (e.g., CRISPR-Cas9), and high-resolution live-cell imaging to dissect and therapeutically target these pathways, ultimately restoring effective antitumor immunity in liver cancer.
Abstract: In fibrotic liver environments, chronic liver fibrosis leads to increased extracellular matrix (ECM) stiffness that, together with cytokine signaling, activates mechanotransduction pathways in tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs). Our revised hypothesis posits that heightened ECM stiffness not only engages integrin β5‐mediated FAK/MEK/ERK signaling but also activates the YAP/TAZ pathway. This dual activation upregulates transcription factors such as HIF‐1α and modulators like LOXL2, thereby reprogramming TAM metabolism toward enhanced fatty acid oxidation and glycolysis. The resulting metabolic shift elevates PD‐L1 expression, suppressing CD8+ T cell cytotoxicity and facilitating tumor progression. By leveraging cutting-edge technologies—including tunable 3D hydrogels, CRISPR-mediated gene modulation, and high-resolution live-cell imaging—we propose targeted inhibition of these mechanotransduction routes as a strategy to reprogram TAM functions, restore T cell activity, and enhance the efficacy of immunotherapies in liver cancer.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis linked ECM stiffness to TAM immunosuppression via integrin‐mediated FAK/MEK/ERK signaling leading to PD‐L1 upregulation. The revised hypothesis retains this core causal chain but incorporates additional mechanotransduction (YAP/TAZ signaling) and acknowledges the interplay with cytokine networks, thereby aligning more closely with current evidence. Additionally, it enhances practical implementability by suggesting the use of contemporary technological approaches (e.g., tunable hydrogels and CRISPR technologies) to specifically dissect and target the proposed mechanistic pathways.
